newsitem.title: JAPAN: Elite school spawns rivals for Japan Premiership.
newsitem.headline: Elite school spawns rivals for Japan Premiership.

text.p: Three decades ago, the main contenders in Japan's general election strolled the halls of the same elite university.

Ryutaro Hashimoto, prime minister and president of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), and Ichiro Ozawa, head of Shinshinto (the New Frontier Party), graduated seven years apart from Keio University, which is better known for producing businessmen than politicians.
Hashimoto, 59, is a 1960 law graduate and a believer in working within the system; Ozawa, 54, a 1967 economics alumnus who would tear down structures that have served him well.
Voters decide in Sunday's general elections which of the pair they would prefer to lead them into the 21st century.

Both entered politics in their twenties after the deaths of their politician fathers, Hashimoto after a stint with a trading firm and Ozawa after graduate school and a failed law examination. They are the only top politicians on a Keio alumni list studded with corporate presidents.

"Keio graduates have long had a strong presence at the head of large and medium-sized firms, but have not been prominent in politics like Tokyo University and Waseda University alumni," said Keio political science professor Yasunori Sone.

Of Hashimoto's 21 predecessors as prime minister in the post-war era, 11 hailed from Tokyo University, the apex of the national university system. Three post-war prime ministers were from Waseda, Keio's rival among top private universities.

"Tokyo University students tend to be of a bureaucratic mind set as if they expect to rule, while Keio students are closer to the average Japanese," said Masatake Isoyama, a 24-year-old Keio law student.

College connections are key in Japan, where many people keep in touch with even primary school classmates, and where "gakubatsu" -- cliques built around college ties -- are pivotal building blocks of corporate and government power structures.

While the cozy Tokyo University clique that undergirds Japan's "iron triangle" of big business, bureaucracy and conservative politicians is justly famous, the Keio connection runs wide and deep throughout the private sector, Sone said.
"Keio's alumni association is one of Japan's biggest, with a network nearly as wide and influential as those of U.S. Ivy League schools," he said.
While Ozawa has tight ties with some Keio people, Hashimoto has been more assiduous in maintaining ties, attending alumni gatherings and sending telegrams to graduation ceremonies.
On the first day of official campaigning last week, Hashimoto lunched with Yuzo Seto, president of Asahi Breweries and a member of Keio's class of 1953.

Hashimoto waxes nostalgic in his memoirs about his college years. He is a proud product of a Keio club where he perfected his skill at kendo, or traditional Japanese sword fighting, and even wields a wooden sword in a daily LDP television spot.

Ozawa is more guarded about his college memories. But in "Blueprint for a New Japan", the policy manifesto which forms the basis of Shinshinto's platform, he says "dull classes" and an "ambiguous character" are the reasons " Japanese university education is not highly regarded at home or abroad."
At Keio's campus -- a shaded island in a congested Tokyo commercial district -- students say they do not generally look up to politicians but are proud to see native sons do well.
They describe the two rivals in much the way pundits describe their political image.
"I picture Hashimoto as the insider who had everything going his way and Ozawa as the underdog who had to fight even to get into Keio," said Tetsuya Fujino, 24, a politics student.
